messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus Volkov, forty-nine, sits in the leather chair across from the therapist with his shoulders drawn inward, his hands folded tightly in his lap. He is a city council member in a mid-sized Midwestern city—the kind of position that demands visibility, composure, a steady hand at community meetings and ribbon cuttings. For the past eighteen months, he has been drowning.

It began on a patrol in Kandahar in 2009. Marcus was a captain then, leading a convoy through a market district. The intelligence had been solid—or so they'd been told. He remembers the weight of the body armor, the dust in his throat, the way the market had gone quiet all at once. Then the IED detonated beneath the second Humvee. He remembers screaming, the smell, the shape of something that might have been a leg. But when he tries to reconstruct the sequence—who was where, what he did in the first seconds, whether he called for the medic or whether someone else did—the memory fractures. Whole stretches are simply gone, replaced by a kind of white noise. Three soldiers died. He knows this. He knows he was there. But the specifics slip away like water through his hands, and when he tries to speak about it, even to himself in the privacy of his home, the words dissolve mid-sentence and he is left gasping, the terror of that moment flooding back into his chest as though it were happening now.

The terror is the worst part. When he forces himself to remember—when he sits alone and tries to piece together what happened—his body responds as if the threat is immediate and real. His heart races. His breathing becomes shallow. His muscles tense as though preparing to dive for cover. Marcus had come to believe that his body was working against him, that it was fundamentally broken, still wired for a danger that no longer existed. He was certain the world remained as lethal as it had been in that market, that safety was an illusion people told themselves. The hypervigilance was constant. He had to be watching, always, for the signs that something was about to go wrong. His wife, Elena, had stopped trying to touch him months ago. When she reached for his arm during dinner or placed a hand on his shoulder in the kitchen, he would flinch violently, his entire body recoiling as though from a live wire. The look on her face each time—a mixture of hurt and resignation—had become another thing he couldn't bear to remember.

To manage the intrusions, Marcus had developed a system. The moment a memory threatened to surface, or when his thoughts began spiraling into catastrophic loops about what might happen if he let his guard down, he would turn on the television or blast music through the speakers in his home office. The noise was a wall. It kept the fragments at bay, filled the spaces where the memories might take hold. At first it had worked—the distraction bought him hours of relative peace. But over time, the strategy had begun to backfire. The sensory flooding seemed to intensify his sense that he couldn't trust anything, that even in his own home he needed external noise to keep himself from dissolving. The constant monitoring of his own thoughts—the exhausting surveillance of his own mind for signs of breakdown—had become its own form of torture. He would catch himself spiraling and then begin monitoring that spiral, watching himself for evidence of losing control, which only deepened his conviction that his mind, like his body, was no longer reliable. When the noise stopped, when he was forced into silence, the fragmented images would rush back with even more force, and his appraisals about the world's danger would crystallize into certainty.

The sleep had gone first. He would lie awake until two or three in the morning, unable to shut off the vigilance, unable to trust that the house was secure even though he had checked the locks four times. Elena had moved to the guest room six months ago. At city council meetings, he found himself struggling to concentrate, his mind half-listening to constituents while the other half monitored the room for exits, for threats, for the moment when everything would fall apart. Two weeks ago, during a public forum about zoning regulations, he had blanked mid-sentence, unable to find his way back to what he had been saying. The silence had stretched. People had stared. He had excused himself and driven home, where he sat in the dark with the television blaring, unable to move.

It was Elena who finally insisted he seek help. She had found him that evening, still in his coat, still in the dark, and she had said something that cut through the noise: "I can't reach you anymore." Marcus knows she is right. He is terrified that if he stops the distraction, stops the monitoring, stops the avoidance, the memories will consume him entirely. But he is also beginning to understand that the very things he has done to survive are now the things that are destroying his life.
